Mapping in R

Understanding spatial data and making a good map with sf

Author

NC State University Libraries — Data Science Services

Published

September 24, 2026

Welcome & learning objectives

Most people who come to a mapping session have the same goal: I have some locations — study sites, sample points, buildings — and I want a decent map of them. That’s exactly what we’ll do. Along the way you’ll pick up the few concepts that make spatial data behave.

By the end of this hour you will be able to:

  1. Explain what makes data “spatial” — geometry, coordinate reference systems (CRS), and the fact that an sf object is just a data frame with a geometry column.
  2. Get your data into R — whether it’s a shapefile, a geodatabase, or a spreadsheet of coordinates.
  3. Ask a question only spatial data can answer — draw a buffer around each landmark, count what falls inside, and find the shadiest spot on campus.
  4. Make a publication-quality map you’d actually put in a poster or paper.

We’ll use real campus data — building footprints (polygons), NC State’s tree inventory (points), and a short spreadsheet of well-known campus spots — and we’ll use it to answer one concrete question: which place on campus has the most trees around it?

NoteFacilitator notes — one-hour timing

Budget ~45 min of content, ~15 for questions and install triage.

Min Section
0–5 Intro + the question we’re going to answer
5–18 §1 Get four files in (.shp, .gdb, .xls, .csv) and clip
18–26 §2 What makes data spatial (anatomy, CRS)
26–38 §3 Explore + the spatial question (buffer + count)
38–52 §4 Making the map — the main event
52–60 Wrap-up, resources, questions

Two things worth slowing down for: the CRS discussion in §2.3 (every downstream headache traces back to it) and building the map layer-by-layer in §4 (that’s the skill everyone came for).

§1 is the tight spot. Four file formats is a lot of reading-in before anybody sees a map. Don’t live-type it — run the chunks and talk over them. The one to actually slow down on is §1.5, st_as_sf() on the CSV, because that’s the on-ramp most attendees need for their own data.

If you run long, §3’s buffer table is the part that has to survive — §4’s map is about that result. The buffer-viz context map is the one to cut.

Before class: confirm the data folder downloads and reads on the room’s setup, and set the repo link in §1. Ask everyone to run install.packages(c("sf", "readxl", "ggspatial")) beforehand.

The punchline, don’t spoil it early: the Court of North Carolina wins and the Brickyard comes last. Both are obviously right to anyone who has walked across campus, which is exactly the point — get the room to guess before you run the chunk.

Setup

Packages we will use:

  • sf — the modern standard for vector spatial data (points, lines, polygons).
  • dplyr — attribute wrangling. sf objects work with filter(), mutate(), count(), group_by() directly.
  • ggplot2 + ggspatial — mapping. geom_sf() draws geometry; ggspatial adds the scale bar and north arrow.
  • readxl — reads .xls/.xlsx straight into a data frame, for the attribute table we join on.
TipA note on the ecosystem

If you go hunting for tutorials, you’ll find old code using sp, rgdal, rgeos, or maptools. Those were retired from CRAN at the end of 2023. Today’s world is sf for vector data. If a Stack Overflow answer loads rgdal, it’s stale — move on.

Rather than assume those are already installed, check first and install whatever’s missing. This is a snippet worth keeping in your back pocket — it’s the difference between a script that runs on your machine and one that runs on a colleague’s.

pkgs <- c("sf", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "ggspatial", "readxl")

# `%in%` against the installed list tells us what's absent; install only those.
missing <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]

if (length(missing) > 0) {
  message("Installing: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
  install.packages(missing, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggspatial)
library(readxl)
NoteWhy it’s written this way
  • Install only what’s missing. Calling install.packages() unconditionally re-downloads and recompiles packages you already have — which for sf means several slow minutes, and on a shared machine may fail outright on permissions.
  • Name the repo explicitly. repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org" means the line also works when R is running non-interactively — in a render, a scheduled job, or CI — where there’s no mirror set and no one to answer the “choose a CRAN mirror” prompt.
  • Still call library() one per line. The install block is plumbing; the library() calls are documentation. Anyone reading your script should be able to see the dependencies at a glance.

A caveat worth knowing: this handles missing packages, not outdated ones. If a package is installed but too old for the code, you’ll get a confusing error rather than an install. packageVersion("sf") is how you check.

1 Get the workshop data

Before we write any analysis, everyone needs the same datasets in the same place.

1.1 What you already have

You downloaded this file as part of the workshop zip, so the data came with it — it’s in the data/ folder sitting next to this document:

  • BLDGSCAMPUS.shp — campus building footprints. A shapefile is actually several files (.shp, .dbf, .shx, .prj, …) that must stay together in the same folder.
  • NCSU_TreeInventory/NCSU_TreeInventory.gdb — the campus tree inventory, as an Esri File Geodatabase. A .gdb is a folder, not a single file — keep it intact, don’t rename what’s inside.
  • CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.shp — the campus precinct boundaries. We use these to clip everything down to main campus.
  • NCStateBuildingsData.xls — building names and addresses, to join onto the footprints.
  • NCState_places.csv — a short list of well-known campus spots as lat/lon coordinates.

One thing to do first, if you haven’t already — and it differs by editor:

  • RStudio: double-click mapping-r.Rproj in the unzipped folder.
  • Positron: launch Positron first, then File → Open Folder and choose the unzipped mapping-r-main folder. (Double-clicking the .Rproj doesn’t reliably launch Positron.)

Either route points R at the project folder, which is what makes the short relative paths below work. Then run this to confirm:

list.files("data")                     # BLDGSCAMPUS.shp, CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.shp,
 [1] "BLDGSCAMPUS.cpg"          "BLDGSCAMPUS.dbf"         
 [3] "BLDGSCAMPUS.prj"          "BLDGSCAMPUS.shp"         
 [5] "BLDGSCAMPUS.shx"          "CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.cpg" 
 [7] "CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.dbf"  "CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.prj" 
 [9] "CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.shp"  "CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.shx" 
[11] "NCState_places.csv"       "NCStateBuildingsData.xls"
[13] "NCSU_TreeInventory"      
                                       # NCStateBuildingsData.xls, NCState_places.csv
list.files("data/NCSU_TreeInventory")  # should include the .gdb folder
[1] "Disclaimer.txt"         "NCSU_TreeInventory.gdb"

Empty, or an error? You’re almost certainly in the wrong working directory rather than missing the files. getwd() shows where R thinks it is; opening mapping-r.Rproj is the fix.

(Need the files again later, or want to follow along after today? Everything lives at https://github.com/NCSU-Libraries/mapping-r — or use the short link from the slides.)

1.2 Read the data into R

st_read() reads dozens of formats the same way — shapefiles, GeoPackage (.gpkg), GeoJSON, and geodatabases. The building footprints are a shapefile, so they read in one call:

buildings <- st_read("data/BLDGSCAMPUS.shp") |>
  st_zm()     # drop the unused elevation coordinate — see the callout below
Reading layer `BLDGSCAMPUS' from data source 
  `/Users/swbrown/workshops/mapping-r/data/BLDGSCAMPUS.shp' using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
Simple feature collection with 1217 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY, XYZ
Bounding box:  xmin: 615828.2 ymin: -467645 xmax: 21530560 ymax: 15950860
z_range:       zmin: 0 zmax: 694.0932
Projected CRS: NAD83 / North Carolina (ftUS)

The tree inventory is a File Geodatabase. Because a .gdb can hold several layers, you point st_read() at the folder and name the layer you want. st_layers() lists what’s inside so you can grab the exact name:

st_layers("data/NCSU_TreeInventory/NCSU_TreeInventory.gdb")
Driver: OpenFileGDB 
Available layers:
                   layer_name geometry_type features fields
1 NCSU_TreeInventory_20251107      3D Point     4424      9
2      NCSU_TreeInventory_OLD      3D Point    12640      9
                       crs_name
1 NAD83 / North Carolina (ftUS)
2 NAD83 / North Carolina (ftUS)
trees <- st_read(
  "data/NCSU_TreeInventory/NCSU_TreeInventory.gdb",
  layer = "NCSU_TreeInventory_20251107"
) |>
  st_zm()
Reading layer `NCSU_TreeInventory_20251107' from data source 
  `/Users/swbrown/workshops/mapping-r/data/NCSU_TreeInventory/NCSU_TreeInventory.gdb' 
  using driver `OpenFileGDB'
Simple feature collection with 4424 features and 9 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XYZ
Bounding box:  xmin: 2087433 ymin: 731473.5 xmax: 2100259 ymax: 746376.2
z_range:       zmin: 0 zmax: 168.1074
Projected CRS: NAD83 / North Carolina (ftUS)
Warningst_zm() — do this now, or debug it later

Both of these layers were exported from ArcGIS carrying a third coordinate, elevation, that nothing in this workshop uses. st_zm() strips it off.

Skip it and everything looks fine: the layers read, print, and plot perfectly happily. Then a clip or an overlay several steps later dies with OGR: Corrupt data / Error: OGR error and no hint as to which line is at fault. Check any layer with class(st_geometry(buildings)[[1]]) — XYZ means the Z coordinate is still attached, XY means you’re clean.

TipReading a .gdb directly — no ArcGIS export needed

sf reads File Geodatabases natively (via GDAL’s OpenFileGDB driver), so there’s no need to export to shapefile first. That’s a good thing: shapefiles truncate field names to 10 characters and flatten some data types, so your attributes are safer straight from the .gdb. If you’re ever choosing a format for your own data, GeoPackage (.gpkg) is the friendly modern option.

1.3 Focus on main campus

The building and tree layers cover all of NC State’s property — including farms and field labs an hour from Raleigh. We want the walkable core, so we’ll clip everything to main campus: the North and Central precincts together. First read in the perimeter shapefile, using the approach above, and work out which column holds the precinct names.

perimeters <- st_read("data/CAMPUSPERIMETER_ALL.shp")   # <- your filename

[6] "Shape_STLe" "geometry"

  OBJECTID   SUM_SUM_Ar Shape_Leng        Precinct_N Shape_STAr Shape_STLe
1       42   1116.82690   60772.11 Centennial Campus   48648815   60771.80
2       43    300.51646   26552.02    Central Campus   13090497   26552.02
3       44   1991.32997   87336.74      Lake Wheeler   86742334   87336.74

The attribute Precinct_N is what we need. North Campus and Central Campus together are what people mean by main campus, so we’ll keep both and clip the other layers to them.

main_campus <- perimeters |>
  filter(Precinct_N %in% c("North Campus", "Central Campus"))

# Keep only features that fall on main campus. Subsetting one sf object by
# another — `layer[boundary, ]` — keeps the features that intersect it. We
# transform the boundary into each layer's CRS on the fly, so this works even
# though the files were saved in different coordinate systems.
buildings <- buildings[st_transform(main_campus, st_crs(buildings)), ]
trees     <- trees[st_transform(main_campus, st_crs(trees)), ]

# The inventory flags trees that have been taken out. We're about to ask a
# question about shade, so the removed ones shouldn't count.
trees <- trees |> filter(spacestatus != "Removed")

nrow(buildings)   # 209 footprints
[1] 209
nrow(trees)       # 1,925 standing trees
[1] 1925

Clipping early, in one place, is what keeps the rest of the session fast and the maps legible — that took us from 4,424 trees statewide down to the 1,925 on the blocks we actually care about.

1.4 Join the building attributes

A quick look at the building attributes — there is not much to see: an internal ID, a building number, and the geometry column:

names(buildings)     # "OBJECTID", "BLDGNUM", "geometry"
[1] "OBJECTID" "BLDGNUM"  "geometry"

The buildings dataset only includes the building footprints and a building number. We will join this dataset with building attribute data in an excel spreadsheet.

bldg_attrs <- read_excel("data/NCStateBuildingsData.xls")

names(bldg_attrs)    # BLDG_NUM, BLDG_NAME, STATUS_DESCR, SITE_DESCR, ADDRESS, ...
 [1] "BLDG_NUM"         "BLDG_NAME"        "STATUS_DESCR"     "SITE_DESCR"      
 [5] "ADDRESS"          "CITY"             "STATE"            "ZIP"             
 [9] "BLDG_COUNTRY"     "BLDG_COUNTY_NAME"
# An attribute join is plain dplyr — nothing spatial about it. Keep the sf
# object on the LEFT and the result is still sf, with geometry untouched.
buildings <- buildings |>
  left_join(bldg_attrs, by = c("BLDGNUM" = "BLDG_NUM")) |>
  rename(name = BLDG_NAME)     # a short name field for the map labels later

# Sanity check: how many footprints failed to find a match? (should be 0)
sum(is.na(buildings$name))
[1] 0
buildings |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(BLDGNUM, name, SITE_DESCR, ADDRESS) |>
  head()
  BLDGNUM                          name SITE_DESCR               ADDRESS
1    127P  King Village Beaufort Hall P    Central      3820 Jackson St.
2    127Q King Village Edgecombe Hall Q    Central      3930 Jackson St.
3     001  Gregg Museum of Art & Design      North 1903 Hillsborough St.
4    170A          Booster Pump Station    Central        3051 Ligon St.
5    127C      King Village Hyde Hall C    Central        2931 Ligon St.
6    127D   King Village Tyrrell Hall D    Central        2941 Ligon St.
WarningJoins fail on key type, not key value

left_join() matches "004" to "004", but never "004" to 4. Campus building numbers are text — they have letters (843B) and leading zeros (004) — so both sides must be character. Open this spreadsheet in Excel and re-save it and Excel will helpfully turn 004 into the number 4, and those rows will silently stop matching. If a join comes back all NA, check class() on both key columns first.

1.5 The third layer — a spreadsheet of landmarks

Our third dataset is the one most people actually arrive with: a plain spreadsheet. A column of latitudes, a column of longitudes, and the job is to turn that table into spatial data. data/NCState_places.csv is exactly that — a hand-typed list of well-known campus spots, and the thing we’ll ask our spatial question about in §3.

places_csv <- read.csv("data/NCState_places.csv")

str(places_csv)     # a plain data frame — no geometry, no CRS, nothing spatial yet
'data.frame':   13 obs. of  6 variables:
 $ name        : chr  "Memorial Belltower" "Brickyard" "Free Expression Tunnel" "Wolf Statues" ...
 $ type        : chr  "Landmark" "Landmark" "Landmark" "Landmark" ...
 $ lat         : num  35.8 35.8 35.8 35.8 35.8 ...
 $ lon         : num  -78.7 -78.7 -78.7 -78.7 -78.7 ...
 $ photo_url   : chr  "https://live.staticflickr.com/8383/29084921961_ea9cd39fa2_z.jpg" "https://live.staticflickr.com/4651/38691306840_bd9cd9a37a_z.jpg" "https://live.staticflickr.com/4571/37535204414_c1c2f0a59a_z.jpg" "https://live.staticflickr.com/4608/40067921452_34dcaba71c_z.jpg" ...
 $ photo_source: chr  "ncsuweb Flickr" "ncsuweb Flickr" "ncsuweb Flickr" "ncsuweb Flickr" ...

Nothing about this is spatial to R. lat and lon are ordinary numeric columns — you could take their mean or draw a histogram of them, and R would not object. One function changes that, and two of its arguments do the real work:

  • coords — which columns hold the coordinates, in x, y order. Longitude first, then latitude.
  • crs — what those numbers mean. You tell R this; it cannot infer it.
places <- st_as_sf(places_csv, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

Read the header: geometry type POINT, CRS WGS 84. Notice that lat and lon are gone from the columns — they were consumed into geometry — while name, type, and photo_url came along untouched. It’s a data frame with a geometry column, exactly like the layers we read off disk.

Worth proving to yourself that the points landed where you meant them to:

# Plotting the points FIRST sets the extent; the boundary then draws into that
# window. Draw the perimeter first instead and campus shrinks to a dot — that
# layer covers NC State property statewide, out to the farms and field labs.
plot(st_geometry(places), pch = 19, col = "firebrick", axes = TRUE)
plot(st_geometry(st_transform(perimeters, 4326)), add = TRUE, border = "grey55")
WarningThe two ways this goes wrong

Reversing coords. c("lon", "lat") is x-then-y, which reads backwards against the “lat/long” everyone says out loud — and this CSV lists lat first, which makes the mistake easier still. Reverse them and R faithfully places campus at 35.8°E, 78.7°S: the middle of Antarctica. Nothing errors. You just get a map of nowhere.

Forgetting crs = 4326. Without it, R stores the numbers but has no idea where on Earth they are, and every later step — mapping, measuring, joining — silently misbehaves. If your coordinates look like -78.6, 35.7, they’re almost always lon/lat, i.e. crs = 4326.

Finally, clip these to main campus the same way we clipped the other two layers:

# The two precinct polygons don't quite meet where the railroad cuts through
# campus, and the Free Expression Tunnel sits in that gap. So we filter on the
# bounding *box* of main campus rather than the polygons themselves, and it
# survives the clip.
campus_box <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(st_transform(main_campus, st_crs(places))))

places <- places[campus_box, ]

places$name     # nine landmarks on main campus
[1] "Memorial Belltower"      "Brickyard"              
[3] "Free Expression Tunnel"  "Wolf Statues"           
[5] "Court of North Carolina" "Hill Library"           
[7] "Talley Student Union"    "Holladay Hall"          
[9] "Reynolds Coliseum"

That on-ramp — table → st_as_sf() → clip → map — is the whole game for coordinate spreadsheets, and it’s exactly how you’d bring in your own study sites.

2 What makes data “spatial”?

2.1 An sf object is a data frame with a geometry column

This is the whole mental model. Print one and you’ll see a normal table with a spatial header on top and a geometry column on the end (its name comes from the source — for our tree data it’s shape):

2.2 Geometry types

Vector data comes in three basic flavors. Our two layers show two of them:

unique(st_geometry_type(trees))      # POINT   — one location each
[1] POINT
18 Levels: GEOMETRY POINT LINESTRING POLYGON MULTIPOINT ... TRIANGLE
unique(st_geometry_type(buildings))  # POLYGON / MULTIPOLYGON — an area
[1] MULTIPOLYGON
18 Levels: GEOMETRY POINT LINESTRING POLYGON MULTIPOINT ... TRIANGLE
# (the third common type is LINESTRING — roads, rivers, paths)

2.3 The coordinate reference system — the one concept that matters most

Every spatial layer carries a CRS: the answer to “what do these numbers mean?” Ask each layer what it’s in — and notice they may not match:

st_crs(trees)$Name       # the tree inventory's CRS
[1] "NAD83 / North Carolina (ftUS)"
st_crs(buildings)$Name   # the buildings' — same, both from campus GIS
[1] "NAD83 / North Carolina (ftUS)"
st_crs(places)$Name      # our spreadsheet — a different CRS entirely
[1] "WGS 84"

There’s the mismatch, live. The two layers that came from campus GIS share a projected CRS in feet; the landmarks we built from a spreadsheet are in WGS 84 degrees, because that’s what we told st_as_sf(). All three are correct. None of them can be overlaid or measured against the others until they’re on a common CRS.

ImportantWhy the CRS is not optional (the conceptual “why”)

Coordinates are meaningless without knowing the system they’re measured in. A pair like (-78.7, 35.6) is a spot in North Carolina only if you know it’s lon/lat degrees on the WGS84 datum. Two things follow:

  • A geographic CRS (e.g. EPSG:4326) measures angles on a globe. A degree of longitude is a different number of meters in Raleigh than at the equator — so you can’t measure distance or area in degrees.
  • A projected CRS (e.g. UTM, or NC State Plane) flattens a region onto a plane in linear units. You reproject to one of these before measuring.

And if two layers are in different CRSs, you must put them on a common one before you can overlay or relate them. We do that next.

3 Explore, then ask one spatial question

3.1 Attribute exploration is just the tidyverse

Because it’s a data frame, ordinary dplyr works. Use st_drop_geometry() when you only care about the attributes — it’s faster and stops the geometry from tagging along through every summary.

3.2 A fast look at the geometry

plot() for a quick glance — but wrap it in st_geometry():

plot(st_geometry(buildings), col = "grey80", border = "grey40")
plot(st_geometry(trees), add = TRUE, pch = 20, cex = 0.4, col = "forestgreen")
WarningGotcha

plot(trees) without st_geometry() draws one map per column — surprising and slow. Always wrap in st_geometry() for a plain map.

3.3 Reproject onto a common CRS (in meters)

We’re about to measure a distance — “within 100 meters” — and you cannot do that in degrees. So we put all three layers onto one projected CRS. UTM Zone 17N (EPSG:32617) is a clean, metric choice for central NC:

trees_m     <- st_transform(trees,     32617)
buildings_m <- st_transform(buildings, 32617)
places_m    <- st_transform(places,    32617)

st_crs(trees_m)$units_gdal    # now "metre" — and all three layers match
[1] "metre"

(If st_crs() ever comes back empty for a layer, its CRS wasn’t recorded — set it with st_set_crs() to the correct code before transforming.)

3.4 The spatial question — which place is the shadiest?

Here is something a plain table simply cannot answer: how many trees are within a hundred meters of the Belltower? Nothing in the tree inventory mentions the Belltower. Nothing in the landmark spreadsheet mentions trees. The only thing relating the two is where they are — which is the whole reason to bother with spatial data.

It takes two steps. Grow each landmark into a circle using a buffer, then count the trees inside it.

# Step 1 — a buffer turns each point into a 100 m circle. `dist` is in the
# CRS's units, which is exactly why we projected to meters first.
shade <- st_buffer(places_m, dist = 100)

# Step 2 — for each circle, which trees fall inside it?
#   st_intersects() hands back a list with one element per circle, holding the
#   row numbers of the trees it contains. lengths() turns that into a count.
shade$n_trees <- lengths(st_intersects(shade, trees_m))

shade |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(name, type, n_trees) |>
  arrange(desc(n_trees))
                     name              type n_trees
1 Court of North Carolina          Landmark      81
2            Hill Library          Building      57
3            Wolf Statues          Landmark      56
4           Holladay Hall          Building      56
5  Free Expression Tunnel          Landmark      54
6      Memorial Belltower          Landmark      43
7    Talley Student Union          Building      35
8       Reynolds Coliseum Athletic Facility      31
9               Brickyard          Landmark      14

The Court of North Carolina takes it with 81 trees, and the Brickyard comes last with 14.

Both of those should feel obviously right to anyone who has walked across campus — the Court is the old tree-lined quad, and the Brickyard is a couple of acres of brick.

Now make the question itself visible:

focus <- st_bbox(st_buffer(places_m, 250))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buildings_m, fill = "grey93", color = "grey84", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = trees_m, color = "forestgreen", size = 0.35, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = shade, fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.10,
          color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = places_m, color = "firebrick", size = 2) +
  coord_sf(xlim = focus[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = focus[c("ymin", "ymax")]) +
  theme_minimal()

Look at where the circles overlap: the tint doubles up, and so does the count. A tree sitting between two landmarks is counted for both — which is correct here, because each question (“how many trees near the Court?”) is asked independently of the others. If you ever needed to assign every tree to exactly one landmark, that’s a different tool: st_nearest_feature().

ImportantThe radius is a decision, not a fact

Change the buffer and you can change the answer. At 50 m the Memorial Belltower wins with 20 trees. At 100 m the Court of North Carolina takes it with 81. At 150 m the Court holds the lead but everything behind it reshuffles. None of those is wrong — they answer subtly different questions: right at the monument versus in the surrounding block.

So pick your radius deliberately, and be ready to justify it. Ours is 100 m because that’s roughly a one-minute walk — about the range over which shade actually influences where you’d choose to sit. Reporting “the shadiest spot on campus” without naming the radius is the spatial-analysis equivalent of a bar chart with no y-axis.

NoteThe vocabulary of spatial relationships

st_buffer() and st_intersects() are two of a family. The others you’ll reach for:

  • st_join(points, polygons, join = st_within) — which region contains each point? (the classic point-in-polygon)
  • st_intersects(), st_contains(), st_touches() — true/false spatial tests
  • st_nearest_feature() — which feature is each point closest to?
  • st_distance() — actual distances between features

Same idea every time: relate features by where they are. That’s what makes the data spatial.

4 Making the map — the main event

We have an answer. Now we need a map that shows it — one map, centered on the winner, carrying three things: the landmark, the buildings around it, and the trees. We’ll build it a layer at a time, naming each cartographic decision as we go.

First, pull out the pieces the map needs:

winner    <- shade |> slice_max(n_trees, n = 1)        # the winning buffer + its count
winner_pt <- places_m |> filter(name == winner$name)   # the landmark itself

# The map window: the 100 m circle plus a little breathing room.
view <- st_bbox(st_buffer(winner, 60))

# Label the halls that actually border the quad — the buildings whose
# footprints touch the circle. Because they touch it they are always inside
# the window, which means no label ever gets clipped at the edge.
edge <- buildings_m[winner, ]
edge$area_m2 <- as.numeric(st_area(edge))
edge_labels  <- edge |> slice_max(area_m2, n = 4) |> st_centroid()

winner$name
[1] "Court of North Carolina"

4.1 Step 1 — geometry on the page

coord_sf() does the zooming. The layers are still all of main campus; we’re only choosing what to look at.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buildings_m) +
  geom_sf(data = trees_m) +
  coord_sf(xlim = view[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = view[c("ymin", "ymax")])

4.2 Step 2 — encode meaning; buildings as quiet context

Buildings recede to grey so the trees read first. The trees are sized by trunk diameter (dbh), which is a fair stand-in for canopy — and therefore for shade, which is what the map is about.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buildings_m, fill = "grey86", color = "grey68", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = trees_m, aes(size = dbh), color = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.4, 3.4), name = "Trunk dia. (in)") +
  coord_sf(xlim = view[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = view[c("ymin", "ymax")])

4.3 Step 3 — draw the evidence, then orient the reader

Two jobs here. The dashed circle is the 100 m buffer from §3 — putting it on the map lets a reader see the rule the claim rests on, instead of taking our word for it. Then the usual map attributes: building labels, a scale bar, a north arrow.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = winner, fill = "#eaf3ea", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = buildings_m, fill = "grey86", color = "grey68", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = winner, fill = NA, color = "grey35", linetype = "dashed",
          linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = trees_m, aes(size = dbh), color = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = winner_pt, color = "firebrick", size = 3, shape = 18) +
  geom_sf_text(data = edge_labels, aes(label = name), size = 2.3, color = "grey30",
               fontface = "italic", check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.4, 3.4), name = "Trunk dia. (in)") +
  coord_sf(xlim = view[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = view[c("ymin", "ymax")]) +
  annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.28) +
  annotation_north_arrow(location = "tr", which_north = "true",
                         style = north_arrow_minimal())
TipLayer order is a design tool

The pale green halo is drawn first, underneath the buildings, so it tints the ground without washing out the footprints on top of it. Put that same layer last and it veils everything beneath it in green. In ggplot2 each geom_sf() paints over the ones before it, so the order you type them is the visual hierarchy.

4.4 Step 4 — the finished, publication-quality map

The last additions are the ones that let the map travel without you: a title that states the finding, a subtitle carrying the number, and a caption crediting the data.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = winner, fill = "#eaf3ea", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = buildings_m, fill = "grey86", color = "grey68", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = winner, fill = NA, color = "grey35", linetype = "dashed",
          linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = trees_m, aes(size = dbh), color = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = winner_pt, color = "firebrick", size = 3, shape = 18) +
  geom_sf_text(data = edge_labels, aes(label = name), size = 2.3, color = "grey30",
               fontface = "italic", check_overlap = TRUE) +
  geom_sf_label(data = winner_pt, aes(label = name), size = 2.9, nudge_y = 26,
                fill = "white", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.4, 3.4), name = "Trunk dia. (in)") +
  coord_sf(xlim = view[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = view[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           expand = FALSE) +
  annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.28) +
  annotation_north_arrow(location = "tr", which_north = "true",
                         style = north_arrow_minimal()) +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("The shadiest spot on campus: ", winner$name),
    subtitle = paste0(winner$n_trees, " inventoried trees within 100 m — ",
                      "more than any other landmark on main campus"),
    caption  = "Data: NC State University, Campus Planning & Strategic Investment · Made in R with sf + ggplot2"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "grey30", size = 10),
    plot.caption    = element_text(color = "grey50", size = 7.5),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

Notice that the title and subtitle are computed from winner, not typed. Change the buffer radius in §3 and the map retitles itself — including if the winner changes.

Save it at print resolution:

ggsave("shadiest_spot.png", width = 8.4, height = 7, dpi = 300)
TipFour cartography habits worth naming
  • Let context recede. Buildings are grey so the trees read first. The eye should land on what the map is about.
  • Draw the evidence. The dashed circle isn’t decoration — it’s the rule behind the claim, put where a reader can check it.
  • Account for what’s missing. dbh is blank for 17 of these trees, and aes(size = dbh) drops them silently (with a warning you’ll scroll past). For anything you publish, decide on purpose: give them a fixed small size, or note the exclusion in the caption.
  • Choose colorblind-safe palettes. This map uses a single hue, so it dodges the issue — but the moment you color by species, reach for viridis or Dark2 and avoid raw red/green contrasts.

5 Wrap-up & where to go next

In one session we went from “what is spatial data?” to a finished map:

  • an sf object is a data frame with a geometry column
  • the CRS tells R what the coordinates mean — check it, and put layers on a common projected CRS before you measure anything
  • data comes in via st_read() (shapefiles, geodatabases), st_as_sf() (coordinate spreadsheets), and an ordinary left_join() for attribute tables
  • clipping to a study area early, in one place, is what keeps a campus map legible
  • st_buffer() + st_intersects() answered a question no attribute table could: which place has the most trees around it
  • geom_sf() + ggspatial turn layers into a publishable map

5.1 Resources

  • Geocomputation with R — free online, the standard reference: https://r.geocompx.org/
  • sf documentation & vignettes — https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/
  • r-spatial.org — news and deeper dives from the maintainers

5.2 Take it further (good exercises)

  • Map your own CSV of sites: read.csv() → st_as_sf() → geom_sf().
  • Re-run the shade question at a different radius and see whether the winner survives it.
  • Rank by canopy instead of by count — swap lengths(st_intersects(...)) for a st_join() and sum(dbh, na.rm = TRUE) per landmark. Does the Brickyard’s handful of big trees change its standing?
  • Flip the question with st_nearest_feature(): assign every tree to its closest landmark, then count().
  • Color the trees by species (aes(color = common)) — you’ll need to lump the long tail into “Other” first, or the legend will run off the page.

5.3 Bonus — putting your points on a basemap

We didn’t cover this in the hour, but it’s the most common follow-up question: how do I get my points on top of satellite imagery, or a street map?

The current go-to is maptiles, paired with tidyterra for the drawing. There’s no single package in R, but maptiles is actively maintained, covers a long list of providers, and does the one thing that used to be painful: it hands back a raster already reprojected into your layer’s CRS, so you don’t have to think about Web Mercator at all.

install.packages(c("maptiles", "tidyterra"))
library(maptiles)
library(tidyterra)

# get_tiles() wants an area, so hand it the view box from §4.
view_area <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(st_buffer(winner, 60)))

sat <- get_tiles(view_area, provider = "Esri.WorldImagery", zoom = 18, crop = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data = sat, maxcell = Inf) +      # the tiles go FIRST, underneath
  geom_sf(data = winner, fill = NA, color = "white",
          linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(data = trees_m, aes(size = dbh), color = "yellow", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_sf(data = winner_pt, color = "firebrick", size = 3.5, shape = 18) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.4, 3.2), name = "Trunk dia. (in)") +
  coord_sf(xlim = view[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = view[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           expand = FALSE) +
  labs(caption = get_credit("Esri.WorldImagery")) +     # attribution is not optional
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA))

Worth doing once just to see it: the inventory points land on top of the actual tree canopy in the imagery, which is a far more convincing argument that your data is right than any table.

Four things that trip people up:

  • The tile layer goes first. geom_sf() layers paint in the order you add them, so a basemap added last covers your data.
  • Attribution is a license condition, not a nicety. get_credit("<provider>") returns the exact string the provider requires — put it in labs(caption = ...).
  • zoom is a trade-off. Higher is sharper and slower, and pulls more tiles from someone else’s server. For a campus-block view, 17–18 is about right; for a whole city, 12–13.
  • Set the plot background explicitly. theme_void() leaves it transparent, and a transparent PNG shows up black in some viewers — which will eat your title and your attribution line.
WarningMost of the good-looking providers now want an API key

This has changed recently enough that a lot of tutorials are wrong about it.

  • Keyless, works today: "Esri.WorldImagery" (satellite), "OpenStreetMap" (streets — it even labels the Court of North Carolina and the halls around it), and the other Esri.* styles. Note that "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas" returns “Map data not yet available” at campus zoom levels, so it’s no use for a close-in map.
  • Key required: all the CartoDB.* styles (including Positron and DarkMatter), every Stadia.* style — which is where the old Stamen designs ended up — and Thunderforest.*. You still get tiles back, but they’re stamped API KEY REQUIRED right across your map. If you have a key, pass it with get_tiles(..., apikey = "…").

names(maptiles::get_providers()) lists everything available.

5.3.1 A black-background map needs no basemap at all

Since every dark tile provider now wants a key, the easier route to a dark map is to just style one — no account, no network, no attribution to track:

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buildings_m, fill = "grey20", color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = winner, fill = "white", alpha = 0.05, color = "grey75",
          linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = trees_m, aes(size = dbh), color = "springgreen3", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_sf(data = winner_pt, color = "firebrick1", size = 3.5, shape = 18) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.4, 3.2), name = "Trunk dia. (in)") +
  coord_sf(xlim = view[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = view[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           expand = FALSE) +
  annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.28,
                   text_col = "grey80", line_col = "grey80") +
  labs(title = "Court of North Carolina", subtitle = "81 trees within 100 m") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "grey8", color = NA),
    plot.title      = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "grey70", size = 10),
    legend.text     = element_text(color = "grey80"),
    legend.title    = element_text(color = "grey80")
  )

The trick is that on a dark ground every piece of text needs its color set explicitly — title, subtitle, legend, and the scale bar’s text_col/line_col. Miss one and it stays near-black and vanishes.

5.3.2 Other routes worth knowing

  • ggspatial::annotation_map_tile() — you already have ggspatial loaded, and this pulls OSM tiles through rosm in a single layer. Fewer providers than maptiles, but nothing extra to install.
  • mapview / leaflet — for a zoomable map in your browser rather than a static figure. The right tool for exploring your own data; the wrong one for a figure in a paper.
